work_completed: `os.killpg(group, 0)` in `_live` raised `OverflowError` for a decimal integer above 1 beyond what `os.killpg` accepts (2**31 and up). That crashed the watch with exit 1 and no envelope.
- `_live` now catches `OverflowError` along with `ProcessLookupError` and counts such a number as an ended group, so it is skipped and named as L5 says.
- The SIGSTOP loop on a trip also catches `OverflowError`. It was already guarded by `_live`, so this is defence in depth.
- I checked every `os.killpg` in the backstop: only the per-poll and start checks go through `_live`, and the SIGSTOP loop is the only other site. `slots.py` also calls `os.killpg`. It is outside my paths and not part of the backstop, so I did not touch it.
- I wrote the unit tests first and saw 4 fail on the old code with the `OverflowError` at `backstop.py:55`.

tests: Two new unit tests, both in `test_w2_157_backstop.py`.
- `test_s4_a_number_no_group_can_have_is_skipped_and_named_not_a_crash` covers 2**31, 2**63 and 10**20 with one live group. It expects a trip, `paused == [live]`, `skipped == [huge]`, and the number named in the log and the inbox item.
- `test_s4_only_numbers_no_group_can_have_end_the_watch_at_once` names only 2**40. It expects no trip, no `nvidia-smi` call, the number in `skipped`, and an `end:` line in the log.
- These plant their own groups only (`start_new_session=True`).

discoveries: The CLI's own type check passes any integer above 1. So only the `OverflowError` path stood between a huge number and a crash, not L1's refusal. A number between 2**31 and 2**63 may behave differently on another libc or kernel, but the `OverflowError` is raised by Python's own conversion, so catching it is portable.
risks: Low. An out-of-range number is now reported as "ended", which is what S4 and the case name expect. A typo that happens to be huge silently counts as ended and still appears in `skipped` and the log, so it is not hidden.
lessons: When a command takes ids from the user, test the integer extremes (2**31, 2**63) as well as 0 and 1.
